title: Big Banks' Third Quarter: JPMorgan Profit Rises 6%, Goldman Sachs Rides an Equities Surge, and Wells Fargo's Credit Costs Jump 51%
summary: Results filed on October 13 show three different pictures: JPMorgan's net interest income up 13%, Goldman's equities revenue up 72% and Wells Fargo's loan loss provision up 51% from a year earlier.
description:
The largest US banks began the third-quarter earnings season on October 13 with results that point in different directions. JPMorgan Chase grew profit modestly, Goldman Sachs posted a large gain driven by stock trading, and Wells Fargo showed solid lending growth alongside a sharp rise in the money it set aside for bad loans. Together the three reports give a useful picture of the American banking system at the start of the final quarter of 2026. The Wells Fargo and Goldman Sachs numbers below come from the companies' own filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission and are described as preliminary. JPMorgan's figures come from two press reports that agree with each other on the main numbers, and readers who need exact figures should consult its official release.

Start with JPMorgan, the biggest of the three. According to RTTNews and a second report from TradingNews, the bank earned net income of about $15.3 billion, or $5.57 a share, up from $14.39 billion, or $5.07, a year earlier. Excluding special items, including net investment securities losses of $658 million, earnings were $5.75 a share. Net revenue was about $50.2 billion, up 8%. Net interest income, which is the difference between what the bank earns on loans and what it pays on deposits, rose 13% to $27.1 billion. Excluding the markets business, it rose 6% to $24.7 billion, helped by higher deposit, credit card and wholesale loan balances, partly offset by lower rates. Noninterest expense rose 12% to $27.3 billion, faster than revenue, because of higher compensation, brokerage and distribution fees, marketing and technology costs. The provision for credit losses was $2.74 billion, made up of $2.2 billion of net charge-offs, which are loans written off as uncollectable, and a net reserve build of $539 million, compared with $3.40 billion a year earlier. One of the reports said the earnings per share missed analysts' consensus of $5.90, and that the return on tangible common equity, a measure of profit against shareholder capital, was 20%. It also said the bank guided to net interest income of about $28 billion in the fourth quarter. These are details from a single secondary source and should be checked against the company release.

Goldman Sachs had the strongest quarter. Its filing shows net revenues of $18.68 billion, up 23% from a year earlier but down 8% from the second quarter. Net earnings were $5.29 billion, up 29%, and diluted earnings per share were $17.01, compared with $12.25 in the third quarter of 2025 and $20.98 in the second quarter of 2026. The annualised return on equity was 18.7%. The main driver was equities, where revenue rose 72% to $6.44 billion on financing and derivatives activity. Investment banking fees rose 21% to $3.22 billion, led by advisory work and equity underwriting. Fixed income, currencies and commodities revenue was $3.47 billion, essentially flat. Asset and wealth management revenue rose 14% to $5.05 billion. Goldman's standardised common equity tier 1 capital ratio, a measure of loss-absorbing capital, was 12.4%, down from 12.9% in the second quarter. The firm declared a dividend of $5.00 a share and repurchased $3.0 billion of stock in the quarter.

Wells Fargo's report is quieter but contains the most important warning. The filing shows net income of $5.95 billion, up 6% from a year earlier and down 7% from the second quarter, and diluted earnings of $1.87 a share, up 13% from a year ago. Revenue was $21.87 billion, up 2% from a year earlier and down 3% from the previous quarter. Net interest income rose 5% to $12.52 billion, while noninterest income fell 1% to $9.35 billion. Average loans grew 11% to $1.03 trillion and average deposits grew 11% to $1.48 trillion. But the provision for credit losses rose 51% from a year earlier to $1.03 billion. The common equity tier 1 ratio was 10.0% on a preliminary basis, down from 10.3% in the second quarter and 11.0% a year earlier. The bank repurchased 28.6 million shares for $2.5 billion, and its efficiency ratio was 63%. Noninterest expense fell 1% to $13.74 billion, and headcount fell 8%. Chief executive Charlie Scharf said the quarter showed broad growth and better returns, and that consumers and businesses remain in good shape, while the bank stays vigilant about risk. Press coverage reported that Wells Fargo shares fell about 3% on the day, with revenue seen as a disappointment, although those reports differed in some details.

What do the three reports say together? First, trading and capital markets are carrying a large share of profit. Goldman's equities revenue and JPMorgan's markets income show that investor activity, including financing and derivatives, remains strong. Second, lending is growing. Wells Fargo's loans and deposits both rose 11%, which suggests demand for credit remains healthy. Third, and more cautiously, credit costs are higher. Wells Fargo's 51% rise in its provision is the clearest sign, while JPMorgan's reserve build was attributed in one report to new lending rather than deterioration. A higher provision means banks are setting aside more money against expected losses, which does not mean those losses have occurred.

For ordinary customers, the main link is through credit. If banks expect more losses, they can tighten standards or price loans higher, especially for credit cards and unsecured loans. If they remain comfortable, borrowing conditions stay roughly as they are. The numbers suggest the second case for now, but the provision trend is worth watching in the fourth quarter. For savers, deposit growth of 11% at Wells Fargo shows that customers are still bringing money to large banks, but rates paid depend on competition and on the Federal Reserve.

For investors, the key point is the difference between the headline and the detail. A profit rise can hide faster cost growth, as at JPMorgan, and a revenue disappointment can hide solid lending, as at Wells Fargo. Capital ratios have also edged lower at Goldman and Wells Fargo, partly because the banks are returning money to shareholders. This article describes company-reported results and is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security.

The remaining big banks report over the coming days, and smaller regional lenders follow. Their credit-loss provisions and commentary on consumer spending will show whether Wells Fargo's rise is specific to that bank or part of a wider pattern.
source_name: Wells Fargo and Goldman Sachs SEC filings; JPMorgan results as reported
image_alt: Office towers in a financial district (illustrative)
key_points: JPMorgan reported third-quarter net income of about $15.3 billion, or $5.57 a share, up from $5.07, with net interest income up 13% to $27.1 billion and noninterest expense up 12% to $27.3 billion.
Goldman Sachs reported net revenues of $18.68 billion, up 23% from a year earlier, net earnings of $5.29 billion and diluted earnings of $17.01 a share, with equities revenue up 72% to $6.44 billion.
Wells Fargo reported net income of $5.95 billion and $1.87 a share, but its provision for credit losses rose 51% from a year earlier to $1.03 billion and its CET1 ratio fell to 10.0% from 11.0%.
Wells Fargo's average loans and deposits each grew 11% from a year earlier, while its headcount fell 8%.
JPMorgan's results are drawn from two press reports that agree on the main figures; Wells Fargo and Goldman figures come from their own regulatory filings and are preliminary.
why_it_matters: Large banks are the first read on whether households and businesses are still borrowing and paying their debts. Strong trading profits can hide slower lending, and a jump in credit costs is an early signal that lenders expect more loans to go bad, which feeds through to what ordinary borrowers are offered.

title: Insider Report Warns European Insurers Are Retreating From Climate Risk, Leaving Homeowners and Governments to Pay
summary: A report based on about two dozen senior insurance professionals says the withdrawal of cover for weather-related losses has begun and will accelerate, while the Association of British Insurers says the industry is investing heavily in understanding risk.
description:
A new report from an insurance industry forum says that the retreat of insurers from weather and climate risks in the UK and Europe has already started and is likely to speed up. The findings, first reported by Bloomberg and republished by Insurance Journal on October 14, 2026, rest on information from about two dozen senior insurance professionals who contributed on condition of anonymity. The report is not a statistical study, and it does not name any European insurer as withdrawing cover. It is best understood as a warning from people inside the industry, which makes it worth reading carefully and with caution.

The report comes from Inside Track, a UK-based nonprofit founded in early 2025 as a forum for industry insiders to share accounts anonymously. According to the article, which was written by Olivia Rudgard and Gautam Naik, Inside Track says it validates its findings through its own research. Some of the contributors were interviewed by Bloomberg. The report also includes a commentary by Lord Nicholas Stern, chair of the Grantham Research Institute at the London School of Economics.

What does it claim? The central finding is that insurers are withdrawing cover for climate-driven risks and moving the losses on to governments and homeowners. The report says some of this retreat has already begun and will now accelerate, increasing uninsured losses that someone else must pay for. It also raises the concern that climate risks are being mispriced. Stern argues that insurers' models have underestimated the danger. A former senior executive at Howden Group Holdings, Anthony Hobley, argues that insurers' pricing expertise is applied mainly to one-year policies, which he says does not help clients manage long-term risk or stay insurable.

Several named executives have spoken in similar terms. Amanda Blanc, the chief executive of Aviva, said in September 2026 that homes being built in the UK today already face uninsurability because of rising flood risk. Günther Thallinger, a board member of Allianz SE, has said that entire regions could become uninsurable because of climate change. These are warnings about the future rather than announcements of specific withdrawals, and the article does not link them to a particular decision by their companies.

The report adds figures on the size of the gap between losses and insurance. Citing the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority, known as EIOPA, the article says only about a quarter of natural catastrophe losses in Europe are currently covered by insurance. In the United States, the article notes, property insurers have scaled back or cancelled policies for wildfire losses in California and hurricane risk in Florida and Louisiana. It also mentions that the Bank of England noted in 2025 that insurers are not always consistent in how they value assets and liabilities when they include climate-related risk. The article gives no further amounts in pounds or euros.

How did the industry respond? The Association of British Insurers said that the industry invests significantly in understanding risk, and that building resilience requires action from government, industry and society as a whole. It also said insurers are subject to robust regulation. Insurance Europe, the European trade body, had not responded in time for publication. These responses matter because the report relies on anonymous sources, and the industry's own account is a necessary counterweight.

To understand why this matters, consider how insurance works. An insurer collects premiums from many customers and pays claims for those who suffer losses. For that to work, the insurer must be able to estimate how likely losses are and price accordingly. When weather becomes more severe and less predictable, the estimates become harder. The insurer can raise premiums, add excesses, narrow what is covered, or decline to cover some properties at all. Each of these protects the insurer, but each also reduces the protection customers receive. Over time, if premiums rise beyond what households can pay, some will drop cover. That is the mechanism the report describes as a shift of risk to homeowners and governments.

There are mitigating factors, which are general background rather than findings of the report. In the UK, a joint government and industry reinsurance scheme called Flood Re helps households in flood-prone areas obtain affordable cover, although its published rules exclude properties built after 2009 and it is due to run until 2039. The exclusion of newer homes is the context for Blanc's remark about homes being built today. Local flood defences, building standards and planning decisions also affect whether a property remains insurable, because insurers price in the protections that exist.

What should homeowners do? Check what your policy covers and what its excesses are for flood and storm, and compare quotes from several insurers or through a broker. Ask whether any flood defences or property-level protection measures, such as flood barriers or raised electrics, can lower your premium. Do not let cover lapse because of a price rise without looking for alternatives, since going uninsured can affect your mortgage terms. Buyers should ask about flood history and check flood risk maps before purchasing.

For policymakers, the report points to difficult choices on land use, public flood defences and whether to support insurance through public schemes. Those choices will determine who carries the cost of climate losses. The report does not offer a settled answer, and readers should treat its forecasts as a view from inside the industry rather than a certainty. The next signals to watch are insurers' renewal pricing, regulators' climate stress tests and any further announcements about areas where cover becomes harder to obtain.
image_alt: Residential street at risk of flooding (illustrative)
key_points: A report from Inside Track, a UK nonprofit, drawing on about two dozen senior insurance professionals in the UK and Europe, says insurers are withdrawing cover for climate-driven risks and that the shift will accelerate.
Lord Nicholas Stern of the Grantham Research Institute argues in the report that insurers' models have underestimated climate danger and that risks are being mispriced.
Aviva chief executive Amanda Blanc said in September that homes being built in the UK today already face uninsurability because of rising flood risk.
Citing EIOPA, the report notes that only about a quarter of natural catastrophe losses in Europe are currently insured.

The Association of British Insurers says the industry invests significantly in understanding risk and that resilience needs action from government, industry and society; Insurance Europe did not respond in time.
why_it_matters: If insurers stop covering flood, storm or wildfire damage, the cost does not disappear. It lands on homeowners, on the banks that lend against homes and on governments that pay for recovery. How the insurance market handles climate risk will affect whether ordinary households can buy a home and keep it protected.

title: SEBI Asks IRDAI to Add Insurance Data to the Consolidated Account Statement for a Single View of Investor Holdings
summary: SEBI chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said on October 15 that the market regulator has written to the insurance regulator, as it also works on adding bank deposit information to the statement investors receive from depositories.
description:
India's market regulator wants investors to be able to see their insurance policies alongside their shares, mutual funds and pensions in one statement. Tuhin Kanta Pandey, the chairman of the Securities and Exchange Board of India, said on Thursday, October 15, that SEBI has written to the chairman of the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India asking that insurance-related information be included in the consolidated account statement, usually shortened to CAS. According to Business Standard, which reported his remarks, he spoke on the sidelines of the annual conference of Sahamati, the industry alliance for account aggregators. The aim is to give investors a fuller picture of their financial holdings. The report does not say when the letter was sent, whether IRDAI has replied, or when any change might take effect.

To see why this matters, it helps to know what the statement is today. A CAS is a combined statement of a person's transactions and holdings across all mutual funds and across securities held in demat form, linked to one Permanent Account Number. According to a guide published by HDFC Mutual Fund, depositories, meaning NSDL and CDSL, generate and send the statement. An investor who has had a transaction in a month receives a statement for that month, and an investor with no transactions receives a half-yearly statement showing holdings. SEBI circulars cited by a market-information site say that email delivery became the default from August 1, 2024, with physical copies available on request, and that from May 14, 2025 fund houses and registrars send their data to the depositories within five days of month-end. The same site reports that SEBI has started discussions with the Reserve Bank of India and IRDAI about widening what the statement covers. Those details come from secondary sources, and readers should check SEBI's circulars for the current rules.

According to the Business Standard report, the statement currently covers securities holdings, mutual funds, stocks held across brokers and the National Pension System. The new request would add insurance. Pandey also said SEBI is working on the technical details of including bank deposit information. That follows an announcement by the Reserve Bank of India that SEBI-regulated depositories can access bank deposit information on a continuous basis. In his remarks, Pandey said the account aggregator framework, which allows people to share their financial data between institutions with their consent, could help link information across products and improve the statement.

Why would a unified view help? Many Indians hold several kinds of financial product at once. A salaried worker may have a bank deposit, a few mutual fund schemes, some shares, a pension account and a life insurance policy, perhaps more than one. Each arrives in its own statement, from a different institution, on a different schedule. People often forget policies, lose track of premium due dates, or do not know the total they have saved. A single statement does not change the products, but it makes the picture easier to see. The report notes that a consolidated view would support financial planning and investment advice based on a person's overall portfolio, for example by showing whether someone who holds a lot of equity also has enough life cover.

Insurance is a different kind of product from shares and funds, which is why the request is notable. A life policy is partly protection and partly savings, and its value is not simply a market price. A term plan has no cash value at all. Showing insurance in a statement designed for investments would require choices about what to display: the sum assured, the premium status, the surrender value or the fund value of a unit-linked plan. The report does not say what SEBI has proposed. India already has a system of electronic insurance accounts held with authorised repositories, which lets policyholders keep policies in one place, and that is a possible starting point for integration, although this is general background and the report does not link the two.

Privacy and consent will be central. Insurance and bank data are sensitive, and the account aggregator framework is built on the idea that the customer approves each sharing of data. A statement that includes insurance would need to respect the same principle and protect the data in transit. The Business Standard report does not discuss these safeguards, so it is not clear how SEBI and IRDAI plan to handle them.

Pandey made several other points at the same briefing. He said SEBI is still in talks with the National Payments Corporation of India, which recently deferred a fee on merchant payments known as the merchant discount rate, and that discussions are ongoing. He said SEBI has sent nearly 44 crore investor-awareness messages over the past nine days, using digital platforms and several languages. He also said SEBI is reviewing proposals to strengthen securities lending and borrowing, which supports short selling, that a working group has met, and that a consultation paper will follow once the proposals are finalised, although he gave no timeline.

What should investors do now? Nothing changes immediately, because the request has not become a rule. In the meantime, there are practical steps. Make sure your mutual fund and demat accounts are linked to the same PAN and the same email address, so that your existing statement is complete. Keep a list of all insurance policies, with the insurer, policy number, premium due date and nominee, and tell your family where it is. Check that nominees are updated across investments and insurance. If you want to see your holdings in one place today, the account aggregator apps that banks and fintech companies offer can already combine some data with your consent.

The next developments to watch are IRDAI's reply, any consultation paper that sets out what insurance data would appear, and the timeline for adding bank deposits. Because the proposal involves two regulators and several industries, it may take time. The direction is clear, however: regulators want investors to see more of their finances in one place.
image_alt: Financial data and charts on a screen (illustrative)
key_points: SEBI chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said on October 15, at Sahamati's annual conference, that SEBI has written to IRDAI's chairman asking that insurance data be included in the consolidated account statement, or CAS.
The CAS today covers securities and mutual fund holdings, and, according to the report, stocks across brokers and the National Pension System.
After the Reserve Bank of India said SEBI-regulated depositories could access bank deposit information continuously, SEBI is working on the technical details to include that data.
Pandey said the account aggregator framework could help link information across financial products and improve the statement.
The report does not give the date of the letter, any response from IRDAI, or a timeline for adding insurance or bank deposit data.
why_it_matters: Most Indian households hold their wealth across mutual funds, shares, pensions, bank deposits and insurance, but see each in a separate statement. A single view would help people plan, and could also make it easier to find forgotten policies and spot gaps in protection.

title: Australian Unemployment Rises to 4.7% as 39,300 Jobs Are Lost, Clouding the Case for Another RBA Rate Hike
summary: September labour force data show the highest jobless rate in about five years, with employment falling when economists expected a gain, just after the Reserve Bank lifted the cash rate to 4.60%.
description:
Australia's labour market weakened in September, handing the Reserve Bank of Australia a harder decision about whether to raise interest rates again. The Australian Bureau of Statistics reported on Thursday, October 15, that the unemployment rate rose to 4.7%, which is the highest in about five years, according to a report by Australian Associated Press carried by Neos Kosmos. August's rate was revised up from 4.6% to 4.7%, so the headline is described by some outlets as steady and by others as a rise, depending on whether they compare with the original or the revised figure. Either way, the rate is up 0.6 percentage points since the start of 2026.

The numbers show a market that lost momentum. Babypips reported that employment fell by 39,300, against a forecast gain of about 19,600 and an August gain of 29,300. The number of unemployed people rose by 8,900. The participation rate, which measures the share of working-age people who are in work or looking for it, fell 0.2 percentage points to 66.8%, below the forecast of 67.0%. Full-time employment rose by 34,400 to about 10.23 million, while part-time employment fell by 73,700 to about 4.55 million. Youth unemployment was 11.1%, up 0.3 percentage points. The trend series, which smooths out month-to-month noise, showed employment up 15,700 and the unemployment rate unchanged at 4.6%. Over the year, employment is up 168,300, or 1.2%. Babypips also noted that hours worked rose 0.1% even as the number of employed people fell 0.3%. Sean Crick, the ABS head of labour statistics, said a higher proportion of people who had previously been outside the labour force moved into unemployment, and that a larger share of people remained unemployed in September than in recent years.

Why is this closely watched? The Reserve Bank raised its cash rate target by 25 basis points to 4.60% on September 30, according to CommBank's newsroom. The decision was unanimous. It was the fourth rise of 2026, taking the total increase to 100 basis points. The board said inflation remains elevated and that some of the upside risks to inflation are materialising. It cited pressure on domestic capacity, the widening conflict in the Middle East, higher global energy prices, and artificial-intelligence-related demand pushing up the prices of technology goods. It also said firms are raising or considering raising prices, and that short-term inflation expectations are elevated. At the same time, it noted that growth has slowed, consumer spending is easing, house prices have fallen in most capital cities and new housing loans have declined noticeably. The RBA left the door open to more increases, saying it will do what is necessary, including raising the cash rate further if needed. CommBank said the effects of earlier increases can take up to 18 months to work through.

Now the jobs data complicate that picture. Babypips said a fifth hike is now harder to justify. A MacroBusiness headline in September, after the August data, said a jump in unemployment would not stop the RBA from hiking, so views on how much the labour market matters differ. The Neos Kosmos report notes that the 4.7% rate is already above the RBA's own forecast of 4.5% for the December quarter, and that RBA staff believe weak productivity has pushed up the unemployment rate needed to keep inflation stable. In other words, the central bank itself has said that Australians may need to accept higher unemployment to bring inflation back to target.

There are two key dates ahead. The September-quarter consumer price index is due on October 28, according to Babypips, and it is the most important input for the Reserve Bank's next decision. The RBA's next meeting is in early November, listed by Babypips as November 2 and 3. CommBank said it still sees risks tilted towards further rate increases, but expects cuts could begin in August or November 2027. That is one bank's forecast and not an official projection.

What does this mean for households? For borrowers on variable-rate mortgages, repayments have already risen after four increases, and the jobs data gives no guarantee that the rises are over. If the RBA pauses, repayments will stay high but stop climbing. For people who are unemployed or worried about their jobs, the priority is to contact lenders early if repayments become hard to manage, because options such as temporary hardship arrangements are easier to arrange before arrears build. For savers, higher cash rates have lifted deposit rates, though banks do not always pass them on in full.

What does it mean for insurers and lenders? Rising unemployment can lead to more mortgage arrears and more claims in some lines, such as income protection and consumer credit insurance. The Reserve Bank's October Financial Stability Review, covered separately in this series, found that most borrowers should cope with harder conditions, but noted pockets of stress, and weaker employment is one factor that could test that judgement. The jobs data alone does not show a rise in arrears, and that evidence would come later.

Monthly labour force data are volatile and are often revised. A single month's fall in employment of 39,300 should not be read as a trend, and the ABS trend estimates show only a small rise in employment. Economists will wait for the October release and for the inflation data before concluding that the labour market has turned. The safest reading is that the labour market is cooling, that inflation remains the central bank's main concern, and that the next two data releases will decide whether the cash rate stays at 4.60%.
source_name: Australian Bureau of Statistics (via AAP and Babypips)
image_alt: Data lines over a globe representing economic statistics (illustrative)
key_points: Australia's unemployment rate was 4.7% in September, the highest in about five years, and August was revised up to 4.7% from 4.6%.
Employment fell by 39,300 against an expected gain of about 20,000; full-time jobs rose by 34,400 while part-time jobs fell by 73,700.
The participation rate fell 0.2 percentage points to 66.8%, and the number of unemployed people rose by 8,900.
The Reserve Bank raised the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.60% on September 30, its fourth rise of 2026 and 100 basis points in total.
The RBA's next meeting and September-quarter CPI on October 28 are the next tests; sources differ on how far the jobs data reduces the chance of another rise.
why_it_matters: Jobs are what pay mortgages. The Reserve Bank has raised rates four times this year to bring inflation down, and a weaker labour market gives borrowers some hope that the increases will stop, but it also means more households face the risk of lost income at the same time as higher repayments.

title: German Insurers' Natural Hazard Losses Reach Only €950 Million in the First Half of 2026, but the GDV Calls It 'Simply Luck'
summary: The German Insurance Association says the low first-half bill reflects the absence of big winter storms, while flood-type losses doubled and the long-term average keeps rising.
description:
Germany's insurers paid out less for natural hazards in the first half of 2026 than their own long-term averages would suggest, and the industry's trade body is warning that this should not be mistaken for good news about the climate. The German Insurance Association, known as the GDV, reported in early September that insured losses from natural hazards in the first six months of the year were about €950 million. The figures were reported by the German trade outlets cash-online.de on September 1 and autohaus.de a few days later, and this article summarises them for English-speaking readers. All amounts are insured losses, meaning the claims that insurers expect to pay, and not the total economic damage.

The breakdown shows where the money went. Storm and hail damage to property accounted for about €400 million. Other natural hazards, such as heavy rain and flooding, were about €200 million, which is roughly double the same period in 2025. Motor insurance natural hazard claims were about €350 million. The total of about €950 million is very close to the first half of 2025, but the mix was different, because in that year storm and hail cost about €500 million and other natural hazards about €100 million, with motor also at €350 million. The GDV describes the half-year as below the long-term average, mainly because there were no major winter storms.

The more notable part is how the association interpreted the result. GDV chief executive Jörg Asmussen said the low losses in the first half were simply luck. The coverage links the comment to climate change and a record-heat summer in 2026, and Asmussen stressed that individual severe weather events can cause high damage at any time. In other words, the figure describes what happened in a particular half-year and not how risky the weather has become.

The GDV also gave a forecast for the full year. For storm and hail, including agricultural crop insurance, it expects about €2 billion in 2026 if the second half is average. A statistically average year, at today's portfolio and price levels, would produce about €3.1 billion. For other natural hazards, such as flooding and heavy rain, it expects about €1 billion for the year, compared with a long-term average of about €1.8 billion. In motor insurance, it expects about 300,000 natural hazard claims and claims spending of €1.2 billion to €1.3 billion, and said the second-half outlook is slightly above average because July brought more damage than usual.

The long-term trend is the central point. According to the GDV figures, the ten-year average of natural hazard losses in property insurance has risen from about €1.4 billion in 2000 to 2009 to about €2.4 billion in 2016 to 2025. That is an increase of roughly 70%, though the reports reviewed do not say whether the figures are adjusted for inflation, rising property values or changes in how many people hold cover, all of which affect claims. The GDV attributes the rise to climate change. Readers should treat the cause as the association's view while recognising that insurers' loss data are one of the main sources used by researchers to track changes in weather damage.

A separate market report published on September 1 by the German financial site Der Aktionär noted that Munich Re shares were the top performer in the DAX that day, up 1.1%, and linked the move to the GDV figures. The author argued that a low loss year can support reinsurers' short-term earnings, while the rising long-term losses underline the importance of adequate premiums. The site disclosed that its publisher holds positions in Munich Re. This is commentary, not a finding, and it is not a recommendation to buy or sell any security.

What is the GDV asking for? According to the reports, the association backs a three-part concept for natural hazard protection. The first is broad but voluntary coverage with an opt-out model, which means that natural hazard cover would be included in building insurance unless the customer chooses to decline it. The second is binding prevention and climate adaptation, including risk-aware planning and building, a construction stop in flood zones, a nationwide natural hazard certificate for buildings, targeted unsealing of land, and a climate risk assessment as part of building permits. The third is a public-private partnership for extreme risks, so that the most severe events are shared with the state. These are the GDV's proposals and not law. Germany has debated compulsory natural hazard insurance for years, and the association's preference for an opt-out model sits between the current voluntary system and a mandate.

What does it mean for homeowners and tenants? Nothing changes in law today. But the debate affects premiums and availability, and there are practical steps. Check whether your building insurance includes cover for natural hazards such as flooding and heavy rain, since standard policies may cover storm and hail but not every kind of water damage. Tenants should check their contents policy. Ask your insurer about measures that can reduce risk, such as backflow protection or flood barriers. If you are buying property, look at official hazard maps.

For readers outside Germany the lesson is general. A single good or bad half-year is a poor guide, and long-term averages and trends matter more. The GDV's own numbers show both a quiet year and a rising baseline at the same time. The second half of 2026 will show whether the association's forecast of about €2 billion for storm and hail holds, and its figures for the full year will be published after the year ends.
source_name: GDV (German Insurance Association), via cash-online.de and autohaus.de
image_alt: Residential houses in a German town (illustrative)
key_points: The GDV puts insured natural hazard losses in the first half of 2026 at about €950 million, roughly the same as the first half of 2025.
Storm and hail losses were about €400 million, other natural hazards such as heavy rain and flooding about €200 million, double last year, and motor insurance about €350 million.

The GDV expects about €2 billion of storm and hail losses for the full year, against about €3.1 billion in an average year, and about €1 billion for other natural hazards against a long-term average of about €1.8 billion.
The ten-year average of property natural hazard losses rose from about €1.4 billion in 2000 to 2009 to about €2.4 billion in 2016 to 2025.

GDV chief executive Jörg Asmussen said the low first-half losses were simply luck, and the association backs broad, opt-out natural hazard cover with binding prevention rules and a public-private scheme for extreme risks.
why_it_matters: A quiet half-year can make climate risk look smaller than it is. The GDV's own numbers show that the long-run average is rising and that single storms or floods can cause large losses at any time, which shapes premiums, planning rules and the debate over compulsory natural hazard insurance.

title: Ontario's Auto Insurance Reform: Opting Out of Accident Benefits Saves About $100 a Year, but Critics Warn of Gaps
summary: Since July 1, several accident benefits are optional in Ontario, and estimates put the saving from declining them all at roughly 5% of an average premium, while victims' advocates say the choice mainly helps insurers.
description:
Ontario drivers renewing their car insurance this autumn face a choice that did not exist a year ago: whether to keep or drop several accident benefits that used to come with every policy. The change took effect on July 1, 2026, and the savings from opting out are modest. Estimates from industry and independent analysts cluster around $100 a year, while victims' advocates warn that the choice carries risks that few drivers will think about until they need the cover. This article explains what changed, with the source for each figure, and does not recommend what any individual should choose.

What changed on July 1? According to Insurance Business Canada, several accident benefits that were mandatory under every Ontario policy became optional. Existing policyholders keep their current coverage at renewal unless they agree in writing to reduce it, and new customers must choose any optional coverage they want. The MyChoice analysis lists the newly optional items as income replacement, non-earner, caregiver, housekeeping and home maintenance, lost educational expenses, expenses of visitors, damage to personal items, and the death and funeral benefits. Some coverages, including dependant care, increased medical, rehabilitation and attendant care, and indexation, were already optional before July. The reform also changed who pays first for treatment. For accidents on or after July 1, 2026, auto insurance generally pays eligible medical and rehabilitation expenses after the public health plan but before supplementary health plans, with medication excluded. Insurance Business reports that auto insurance is now the first payer even when a claimant has group health coverage.

How much can a driver save? Two estimates are available. The Insurance Brokers Association of Ontario estimates that opting out of all the newly optional benefits saves about $100 a year at most, roughly 5% of an average premium of about $2,000. MyChoice, a comparison site, analysed more than 1,000 quotes for a standard profile, a 35-year-old married driver with a clean record, and found that declining all newly optional benefits saved about $106 a year, or $8.83 a month, about 5% of a $2,132 average premium. Income replacement accounted for about $47 of that, housekeeping about $36, caregiver about $10 and non-earner about $8, with most other items about $1 each. MyChoice cautions that its figures are based on quotes and not bound policies or completed claims, reflect only the first month of the new system, and do not represent all drivers. Individual savings will vary.

What are drivers choosing? In the MyChoice sample, 32.6% declined every optional benefit and 67.4% kept at least one. About 64% kept the death and funeral benefits, 52% kept income replacement, while only about 11% kept housekeeping and 10% kept caregiver. The weekly limits in the quotes analysed were $400 for income replacement, $185 for non-earners, $250 for the caregiver benefit for the first dependant and $100 for housekeeping. These are the limits in that sample, and policies can differ.

The critics' case is stated by the Association of Victims for Accident Insurance Reform, known as FAIR. Its board chair, Rhona DesRoches, said the illusion of more choice will only help insurance companies, alleged that insurers lobbied for the changes, and said the changes weaken long-standing consumer protections. She expects the savings to be small and temporary, with premiums rising again later. The Insurance Bureau of Canada, the industry's trade body, calls the reform a move away from a one-size-fits-all model and argues that drivers avoid paying twice for coverage they may already have through work. Brokers' associations broadly support the framework but want strong disclosure at the point of sale, and the Ministry of Finance says the changes give drivers more choice and convenience.

One of the most important facts concerns people who are not drivers. The Insurance Bureau of Canada says about 40% of accident victims do not hold their own auto policy. Passengers, pedestrians and cyclists may therefore rely on the reduced minimum unless the at-fault driver bought optional benefits. That is the context for the advocates' warning. A driver who opts out is also reducing the protection available to others in an accident that driver causes, although the sources do not quantify how often this would matter.

What about premium trends? The Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Ontario data cited by Money.ca show the average annual private passenger premium rose from $1,927 in June 2024 to $2,164 in October 2025, an increase of 13.3%. The Insurance Brokers Association of Ontario puts the rise at more than 12%, and the increases have been driven by repair costs and auto theft. In its article of September 20, Money.ca reported that the regulator had approved rate decreases for nine insurer filings, with renewals taking effect between August 15 and November 28, 2026. The largest average cut was 5.3% from The Personal Insurance Company, effective November 28, and the others ranged from 0.23% for Wawanesa to 4.62% for Heartland Farm Mutual. One insurer, S&Y Insurance Company, was approved for a 1.19% increase effective September 1. The article noted that the regulator has not tied any specific rate filing to the reform. A projection by the consulting firm Oliver Wyman, quoted by MyChoice and assuming 80% take-up, found that the reduction from declining coverage would be offset by higher costs elsewhere, leaving a projected net increase of 0.28% in the required average premium. That is a projection, not an observed result.

What should a driver do at renewal? Read the renewal documents carefully, because existing coverage continues unless you agree in writing to change it. Ask your broker or insurer to list exactly which benefits you would be dropping and what the premium difference is. Check what you already have through an employer plan, including disability and health benefits, and whether those would apply after a car accident. Consider your household: a family with one earner and young children may value income replacement and caregiver benefits differently from a single driver with employer disability cover. Compare quotes from several insurers, and keep a record of any change you approve.

The regulator has urged insurers and brokers to document clearly which coverage is added or removed at each transaction. The first full year of data will show whether premiums fall, whether many drivers regret their choices, and how claims develop. For now, the reform offers a small saving in exchange for a more complicated decision, and the fact that the saving is about $9 a month is a reason to weigh carefully what is being given up.
source_name: Insurance Business Canada, MyChoice and Money.ca (citing FSRA and IBC)
key_points: Since July 1, 2026, several Ontario accident benefits, including income replacement, caregiver and housekeeping benefits, have become optional, and auto insurance now pays medical and rehabilitation costs before group health plans.

The Insurance Brokers Association of Ontario estimates that opting out of all newly optional benefits saves about $100 a year at most, and a MyChoice quote analysis found about $106 a year, around 5% of the average premium.
MyChoice found 32.6% of drivers in its analysis declined every optional benefit, while about 52% kept income replacement.

The Insurance Bureau of Canada says about 40% of accident victims do not hold their own auto policy, so passengers, pedestrians and cyclists may rely on the minimum unless the at-fault driver bought optional benefits.
Ontario's average annual premium rose from $1,927 in June 2024 to $2,164 in October 2025, and FSRA has approved nine filings with decreases of between 0.23% and 5.3%.
why_it_matters: Auto insurance is compulsory in Ontario, and most drivers renew every year, so the choice at renewal affects a large number of households. A small saving can be outweighed by a large uncovered loss after a serious crash, which makes it important to understand what is optional before agreeing to change a policy.
